AEM Electrolyser EL 4.0

Enapter’s patented anion exchange membrane (AEM) electrolyser is a standardised, stackable and flexible system to produce on-site hydrogen. The modular design – paired with advanced software integration – allows set up in minutes and remote control and management. Stack this electrolyser to achieve the required hydrogen flowrate.

Footnotes: None Analysis: The table is a two-column specification grid for the Enapter AEM Electrolyser EL 4.0, with no separate header row. The left column lists 21 specification parameters and the right column gives the corresponding values. It appears in the context of Enapter’s patented anion exchange membrane electrolyser, described as standardised, stackable, flexible, modular, software-integrated, and able to produce on-site hydrogen; the table details the technical basis for stacking units to achieve a required hydrogen flowrate. Key data points: Production rate is up to 500 NL/h, up to 1.0785 kg/24 h. Hydrogen output purity is 99.9% at 35 barg with <1,000 ppm H₂O and <5 ppm O₂ at 25 °C, and 98.8% at 8 barg with <12,000 ppm H₂O and <5 ppm O₂ at 25 °C. Output pressure is up to 35 barg. Nominal power consumption is 4.8 kWh/Nm³ of H₂ produced at beginning of life. Operative power consumption is 2.4 kW beginning of life, peak power consumption is 3 kW, and standby power consumption is 0.3 kW. Heat dissipation is 0.6 kW beginning of life and max heat dissipation is 0.9 kW end of life. Power supply is 220–240 V AC, 50/60 Hz. Maximum water input conductivity is minimum ASTM D1193-06 Type IV or recommended Type II or Type III. Water consumption is ~420 mL/h at 25 °C, and water input pressure range is 1–4 barg. Ambient operative temperature range is 5 °C–45 °C, and ambient operative humidity range is up to 90% humidity, non-condensing. IP rating is IP 20. Dimensions are W: 482 mm × D: 635 mm × H: 266 mm, weight is 42 kg, and space inside cabinet is 6 U. Control and monitoring is fully automatic with Enapter’s EMS via 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, Modbus TCP over Ethernet. Conformity includes CE mark according to machine directive 2006/42/CE, UKCA mark according to Supply Machinery (Safety) Regulations 2008, and CSA/ANSI B22734:2023 Ed.1 Hydrogen Generators Using Water Electrolysis - Industrial, Commercial, and Residential Applications. Statistical insights and trends: The operative power of 2.4 kW is consistent with the nominal power consumption: 4.8 kWh/Nm³ × 0.5 Nm³/h (500 NL/h) = 2.4 kW. The production rate of 1.0785 kg/24 h also aligns with 500 NL/h H₂ using the density of hydrogen at normal conditions (~0.08988 kg/Nm³). Peak power is 3 kW, 25% above operative power, while standby power is 0.3 kW, 12.5% of operative power. Water consumption of ~420 mL/h is close to the stoichiometric requirement for 500 NL/h H₂ (~402 mL/h), indicating a modest excess. Purity decreases at lower output pressure: 35 barg gives 99.9% with <1,000 ppm H₂O, whereas 8 barg gives 98.8% with <12,000 ppm H₂O, while O₂ remains <5 ppm in both cases. Heat dissipation rises from 0.6 kW beginning of life to 0.9 kW end of life, showing degradation over the system lifetime. Relationships between data elements: Production rate, nominal power consumption, operative power, water consumption, and heat dissipation together define the unit’s operating envelope. Output pressure directly influences hydrogen purity. Dimensions, weight, 6 U cabinet space, IP 20 rating, and ambient ranges describe physical integration and installation constraints. Control and monitoring features support the surrounding claim of remote control and management. Conformity marks and footnotes connect the table to safety, pressure equipment, and regional regulatory requirements. Significance in context: The table supports the surrounding content by specifying the modular, stackable AEM Electrolyser EL 4.0. A single unit produces up to 500 NL/h, so stacking multiple units can scale to a required hydrogen flowrate. The electrical, water, ambient, physical, communication, and compliance details show that the EL 4.0 is designed for standardised on-site hydrogen production with remote management. The note that specifications may change due to continuous improvement indicates the table is a technical snapshot, and the footnotes clarify standby definition, battery limits, pressure equipment categories, ETL recognition, and owner manual requirements.
